# Esther Chapter 1 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 456r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_001_page_001.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1:1** Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus — the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces —

**1:2** in those days, when King Ahasuerus sat upon the throne of his kingdom in the citadel of Susa,

**1:3** in the third year of his reign, he gave a banquet for all his officials and servants. The military forces of Persia and Media, the nobles and the governors of the provinces, were assembled before him,

**1:4** and he displayed the riches of his glorious kingdom and the splendor of his excellent majesty for many days — one hundred and eighty days.

**1:5** When those days were completed, the king gave a seven-day feast for all the people present in the citadel of Susa, from the greatest to the least, in the courtyard garden of the royal palace.

**1:6** White and blue-violet linen hangings were fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars. Gold and silver couches stood upon a mosaic pavement of alabaster, marble, mother-of-pearl, and dark stone.

**1:7** Drinks were served in golden vessels, each one different from the next, and the royal wine flowed abundantly, as befitted the king's generosity.

**1:8** The drinking was governed by this rule: no one was compelled, for the king had instructed every steward of his household to serve each guest according to his own desire.

**1:9** Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Ahasuerus.

**1:10** On the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas — the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus —

**1:11** to bring Queen Vashti before the king wearing the royal crown, to display her beauty before the peoples and the officials, for she was lovely in appearance.

**1:12** But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command conveyed through the eunuchs. At this, the king became furious, and his anger burned within him.

**1:13** The king then consulted the wise men who understood the times — for it was the king's custom to consult those versed in law and judgment.

**1:14** Those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan — the seven officials of Persia and Media who had personal access to the king and held the highest rank in the kingdom.

**1:15** "According to law, what is to be done with Queen Vashti, since she has not obeyed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"

**1:16** Memucan answered before the king and the officials: "Queen Vashti has wronged not the king alone, but all the officials and all the peoples throughout the provinces of King Ahasuerus.

**1:17** For the queen's conduct will become known to all women, causing them to look upon their husbands with contempt, saying, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she refused to come.'

**1:18** This very day, the noblewomen of Persia and Media who hear of the queen's conduct will cite it to all the king's officials, and there will be no end of contempt and discord.

**1:19** If it pleases the king, let a royal decree go forth from him, and let it be inscribed in the laws of Persia and Media so that it cannot be revoked: that Vashti shall never again come before King Ahasuerus, and let the king bestow her royal position upon another who is more worthy.

**1:20** When the king's decree is proclaimed throughout his entire kingdom — vast as it is — all wives will give honor to their husbands, from the greatest to the least."

**1:21** This counsel pleased the king and the officials, and the king acted according to the word of Memucan.

**1:22** He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, proclaiming that every man should be master in his own household and should speak in the language of his own people.

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Esther chapter 1 opens the book with deliberate literary extravagance, lavishing attention on the wealth and power of the Persian Empire only to expose its absurdity. The king who rules 127 provinces is undone by one woman's refusal. The council agreed that the chapter's tone is simultaneously grand and satirical — a narrative strategy the Hebrew storyteller employs with consummate skill. Notably, this is the beginning of the only book in the Hebrew Bible that never mentions God by name or title. All three translators concurred that this silence should be preserved without editorial addition, and that divine providence is communicated through the architecture of the plot rather than through explicit theological statement. The decree that "every man should be master in his own household" carries heavy irony: the story will ultimately show a woman — Esther — exercising decisive influence over the most powerful man in the world.

---

## Disagreement Log

**1. Verse 1:4 — "splendor of his excellent majesty" vs. "staggering wealth and splendor"**
- EMET: "splendor [yeqar] of the beauty [tiferet] of his greatness [gedulato]" — preserves each Hebrew noun.
- LOGOS: "the splendor of his excellent majesty" — formal compression.
- PNEUMA: "the staggering wealth and splendor of his kingdom" — interpretive and vivid.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted LOGOS phrasing "splendor of his excellent majesty" as a balanced rendering that retains the grandeur of the Hebrew construction without over-compressing or over-interpreting.

**2. Verse 1:12 — "refused" vs. "Queen Vashti refused"**
- EMET: "Queen Vashti refused [vatemmaen]" — preserves the strong Hebrew verb of refusal.
- LOGOS: "Queen Vashti refused to come" — formal and clear.
- PNEUMA: "Queen Vashti refused to come. The king was humiliated and enraged" — adds "humiliated" (interpretive).
- SOPHIA ruling: Used "Queen Vashti refused to come" (LOGOS). PNEUMA's "humiliated" is a valid inference but is not in the Hebrew text; the text says only that the king was angry [vayiqtzof] and his wrath burned.

**3. Verse 1:22 — "master in his own household"**
- EMET: "ruler [sorer] in his house" — literal.
- LOGOS: "master in his own household" — standard formal equivalent.
- PNEUMA: "the master of his own household" — similar but with definite article.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted "master in his own household" (LOGOS) as the consensus phrasing. The Hebrew *sorer* denotes authoritative rule; "master" captures this without the archaic tone of "ruler in his house."

---

*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
